q: A basement wall is poured against formwork and later backfilled with soil. What minimum cover applies to its 16 mm outer bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: The wall was formed, so it is "exposed to earth", not "cast against earth". Formed surfaces exposed to earth or weather need 40 mm for 16 mm bars and smaller. 75 mm applies only when concrete is poured straight onto soil.

q: A 40 mm bar gets a standard hook. What is its minimum inside bend diameter?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: 40 and 58 mm bars bend around at least 10db: 10 × 40 = 400 mm.

q: An interior suspended slab uses 12 mm bars. What minimum cover applies?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Slabs, walls and joists not exposed to weather need 20 mm for 36 mm bars and smaller. That is why slab bars sit on 20 to 25 mm chairs or spacers.

q: What is development length?
o: The length of a lap splice
The length of a hook's tail
The embedment a bar needs so bond can build up its full design stress
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: Past the point of maximum stress, a bar must be embedded far enough for bond to transfer its force into the concrete. If it is shorter, the bar pulls out before it can yield.

q: A 25 mm bar gets a standard hook. What is its minimum inside bend diameter?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: Bars from 10 to 25 mm bend around at least 6db: 6 × 25 = 150 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum development length of a straight deformed bar in tension, whatever the formula gives?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: NSCP 425.4.2.1 sets ld as the larger of the computed value and 300 mm. The minimum for bars in compression is 200 mm, and for standard hooks the larger of 8db and 150 mm.

q: The bottom of a footing is poured directly on compacted soil. What minimum cover applies to its bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Concrete cast against and permanently in contact with earth needs 75 mm, because the soil surface is rough and moist. Rebar chairs or concrete blocks keep the bars up at that height.

q: Under NSCP 2015, how long must a Class B tension lap splice be?
o: 1.3 times the development length, and at least 300 mm
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.5 Splices
n: Class A splices (1.0 ld) are allowed only where the steel provided is at least twice what is needed and no more than half the bars are spliced there. Otherwise, the usual case, a Class B splice of 1.3 ld is required, never less than 300 mm.

q: A 16 mm tie ends in a 135° hook. How long must the extension be?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: A 135° tie hook needs the greater of 6db and 75 mm. 6 × 16 = 96 mm, which is more than 75 mm, so 96 mm governs.
steps: 96 mm is greater, so extension = 96 mm

q: A 25 mm main bar ends in a 90° standard hook. How long must the straight extension be?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: A 90° hook on a main bar needs a 12db extension: 12 × 25 = 300 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, why do top bars need a longer development length?
o: Bleed water and air collect under bars with more than 300 mm of fresh concrete below them, weakening the bond
Top bars are closer to the formwork
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: As fresh concrete settles, water and air collect under high bars. The factor ψt = 1.3 lengthens ld for horizontal bars with more than 300 mm of concrete cast below them.

q: A column on an open-air deck uses 25 mm bars. What minimum cover applies to the main bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Concrete exposed to weather needs 50 mm for 20 to 58 mm bars. Note that 40 mm is the minimum for interior columns, measured to the ties.

q: Why do epoxy-coated bars need a longer development length?
o: The smooth coating reduces the bond between bar and concrete
The coating makes the bars stronger
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: Epoxy protects against corrosion but lowers bond. NSCP applies ψe = 1.5 (for small cover or spacing) or 1.2 (otherwise), with ψt × ψe capped at 1.7.

q: A 36 mm bar gets a standard hook. What is its minimum inside bend diameter?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: Bars from 28 to 36 mm bend around at least 8db: 8 × 36 = 288 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, which of these does NOT affect the tension development length of a deformed bar?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: ld depends on fy, f'c, bar size, bar location (top bars), coating, lightweight concrete, cover, spacing and confinement. The beam span does not enter the formula.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum development length of a standard hook in tension?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: A hook shortens the anchorage needed, but ldh must still be at least 8db and at least 150 mm.

q: A 10 mm stirrup ends in a 90° hook. How long must the extension be?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: For 16 mm and smaller stirrups, a 90° hook needs the greater of 6db and 75 mm. 6 × 10 = 60 mm, so 75 mm governs.

q: An interior wall uses very large 40 mm bars. What minimum cover applies?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Interior slabs, walls and joists normally need 20 mm, but 40 and 58 mm bars need 40 mm because such large bars need more concrete around them to bond and to split less.

q: What can happen if bars are not developed or spliced properly?
o: Nothing, as long as the bars are large
The bars pull out or the splice slips before the steel yields, causing a brittle failure
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: Anchorage failures happen suddenly, without the warning of yielding steel. Proper development lets the member reach its full, ductile strength.

q: Why does concrete cover matter besides corrosion protection?
o: It gives fire protection and lets the bars bond properly with the concrete
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Cover delays heat reaching the steel in a fire, protects against corrosion, and provides enough concrete around each bar for bond without splitting.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum development length of a bar in compression?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.4 Development of reinforcement (ACI 318-14 Ch. 25)
n: Compression bars develop more easily because they also bear on the concrete at their ends, so their minimum ld is 200 mm, less than the 300 mm for tension.

q: An interior beam has 10 mm stirrups and 20 mm main bars. The cover is measured to which bars, and how much is it?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Interior beams and columns need 40 mm to the outermost steel, which is usually the stirrup. The main bars then sit 50 mm from the surface.

q: A 25 mm stirrup ends in a 90° hook. How long must the extension be?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: For 20 to 25 mm stirrups, a 90° hook needs 12db: 12 × 25 = 300 mm. Such large stirrups usually get 135° hooks (6db = 150 mm) instead.

q: A canopy slab exposed to rain uses 12 mm bars. What minimum cover applies?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 420.6.1.3.1 Cover for cast-in-place non-prestressed concrete
n: Concrete exposed to weather needs 40 mm for 16 mm bars and smaller, twice the 20 mm allowed for interior slabs.

q: A 20 mm main bar ends in a 180° standard hook. How long must the straight extension be?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 425.3.1 and 425.3.2 Hook geometry
n: The extension is the greater of 4db and 65 mm. 4 × 20 = 80 mm, which is more than 65 mm, so 80 mm governs.
